regressor). The columns are linearly independent, so $\mathbf{A}$ has full column rank $p=2$. The column
space $\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{A})$ is the set of all vectors of the form $\beta_0\mathbf{a}_1+\beta_1\mathbf{a}_2$,
that is, every "straight-line" pattern of predicted outcomes; least squares finds the straight line closest
to the data.

**Step 1: Gram-Schmidt.** Set $\mathbf{u}_1=\mathbf{a}_1=(1,1,1,1)^\top$, with $\|\mathbf{u}_1\|^2=4$, so
$\|\mathbf{u}_1\|=2$ and $\mathbf{q}_1=\tfrac12(1,1,1,1)^\top$. For the second column,
$\langle\mathbf{a}_2,\mathbf{u}_1\rangle=1+2+3+4=10$ and $\langle\mathbf{u}_1,\mathbf{u}_1\rangle=4$, so
$$
\mathbf{u}_2=\mathbf{a}_2-\frac{10}{4}\mathbf{u}_1=(1,2,3,4)^\top-\tfrac52(1,1,1,1)^\top
=\bigl(-\tfrac32,-\tfrac12,\tfrac12,\tfrac32\bigr)^\top .
$$
Then $\|\mathbf{u}_2\|^2=\tfrac94+\tfrac14+\tfrac14+\tfrac94=5$, so $\|\mathbf{u}_2\|=\sqrt5$ and
$\mathbf{q}_2=\tfrac1{\sqrt5}\bigl(-\tfrac32,-\tfrac12,\tfrac12,\tfrac32\bigr)^\top$. One checks
$\langle\mathbf{q}_1,\mathbf{q}_2\rangle=\tfrac1{2\sqrt5}(-\tfrac32-\tfrac12+\tfrac12+\tfrac32)=0$, as the
theorem promises. Subtracting the multiple of $\mathbf{u}_1$ has *centered* the regressor: $\mathbf{u}_2$ is
the covariate with its mean removed.

**Step 2: QR factorization.** The factor entries are $r_{11}=\|\mathbf{u}_1\|=2$,
$r_{12}=\langle\mathbf{a}_2,\mathbf{q}_1\rangle=\tfrac12(1+2+3+4)=5$, and $r_{22}=\|\mathbf{u}_2\|=\sqrt5$.
Thus
$$
\mathbf{Q}=\begin{bmatrix}
\tfrac12 & -\tfrac{3}{2\sqrt5}\\[2pt]
\tfrac12 & -\tfrac{1}{2\sqrt5}\\[2pt]
\tfrac12 & \tfrac{1}{2\sqrt5}\\[2pt]
\tfrac12 & \tfrac{3}{2\sqrt5}
\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\mathbf{R}=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 5\\ 0 & \sqrt5\end{bmatrix}.
$$
The diagonal of $\mathbf{R}$ is positive, so this is the unique reduced QR factorization of
@thm-qr. To verify, $\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{R}$ has first column $2\mathbf{q}_1=(1,1,1,1)^\top=\mathbf{a}_1$ and
second column $5\mathbf{q}_1+\sqrt5\,\mathbf{q}_2=(\tfrac52,\tfrac52,\tfrac52,\tfrac52)^\top
+(-\tfrac32,-\tfrac12,\tfrac12,\tfrac32)^\top=(1,2,3,4)^\top=\mathbf{a}_2$.

**Step 3: Normal equations.** Compute the Gram matrix and right-hand side,
$$
\mathbf{A}^\top\mathbf{A}=\begin{bmatrix}4&10\\10&30\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\mathbf{A}^\top\mathbf{b}=\begin{bmatrix}1+3+4+4\\ 1+6+12+16\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}12\\35\end{bmatrix}.
$$
Here $\det(\mathbf{A}^\top\mathbf{A})=4\cdot30-10\cdot10=20\ne0$, confirming invertibility (full column
rank), and
$$
(\mathbf{A}^\top\mathbf{A})^{-1}=\frac{1}{20}\begin{bmatrix}30&-10\\-10&4\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\hat{\mathbf{x}}=(\mathbf{A}^\top\mathbf{A})^{-1}\mathbf{A}^\top\mathbf{b}
=\frac{1}{20}\begin{bmatrix}30\cdot12-10\cdot35\\ -10\cdot12+4\cdot35\end{bmatrix}
=\frac{1}{20}\begin{bmatrix}10\\20\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\tfrac12\\1\end{bmatrix}.
$$
So the best-fitting line has intercept $\tfrac12$ and slope $1$: each one-unit increase in the covariate is
associated with a one-unit increase in predicted outcome.

**Step 4: the same answer by QR.** With $\mathbf{Q}^\top\mathbf{b}=(\mathbf{q}_1^\top\mathbf{b},\mathbf{q}_2^\top\mathbf{b})^\top$:
$\mathbf{q}_1^\top\mathbf{b}=\tfrac12(1+3+4+4)=6$ and
$\mathbf{q}_2^\top\mathbf{b}=\tfrac1{\sqrt5}\bigl(-\tfrac32\cdot1-\tfrac12\cdot3+\tfrac12\cdot4+\tfrac32\cdot4\bigr)
=\tfrac1{\sqrt5}(-\tfrac32-\tfrac32+2+6)=\tfrac{5}{\sqrt5}=\sqrt5$. Back-substitution in
$\mathbf{R}\hat{\mathbf{x}}=\mathbf{Q}^\top\mathbf{b}$, that is
$\begin{bmatrix}2&5\\0&\sqrt5\end{bmatrix}\hat{\mathbf{x}}=\begin{bmatrix}6\\\sqrt5\end{bmatrix}$, gives
$\sqrt5\,\hat x_2=\sqrt5\Rightarrow\hat x_2=1$ and then $2\hat x_1+5=6\Rightarrow\hat x_1=\tfrac12$,
matching Step 3 exactly. Two routes, one fitted line.

**Step 5: projection, residual, and orthogonality.** The fitted vector is
$$
\hat{\mathbf{y}}=\mathbf{A}\hat{\mathbf{x}}=\tfrac12\mathbf{a}_1+1\cdot\mathbf{a}_2
=\bigl(\tfrac32,\tfrac52,\tfrac72,\tfrac92\bigr)^\top=P_{\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{A})}\mathbf{b},
$$
the model-predicted outcomes, and the residual is
$\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{b}-\hat{\mathbf{y}}=\bigl(-\tfrac12,\tfrac12,\tfrac12,-\tfrac12\bigr)^\top$, the part of
each outcome the line cannot explain. The orthogonality guaranteed by @thm-projection-theorem is visible:
$$
\langle\mathbf{r},\mathbf{a}_1\rangle=-\tfrac12+\tfrac12+\tfrac12-\tfrac12=0,
\qquad
\langle\mathbf{r},\mathbf{a}_2\rangle=-\tfrac12+1+\tfrac32-2=0,
$$
so $\mathbf{r}\in\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{A})^\perp=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{A}^\top)$. In applied language, the first
identity says the residuals sum to zero, and the second says the residuals are uncorrelated with the
covariate: the two diagnostics any analyst checks after a regression. The residual sum of squares is
$\mathrm{RSS}=\|\mathbf{r}\|^2=4\cdot\tfrac14=1$. Since $\bar b=\tfrac{12}{4}=3$, the total sum of squares is
$\mathrm{TSS}=\|\mathbf{b}-\bar b\,\mathbf{1}_4\|^2=(-2)^2+0^2+1^2+1^2=6$, giving the coefficient of
determination $R^2=1-\mathrm{RSS}/\mathrm{TSS}=1-\tfrac16=\tfrac56\approx0.833$: the line explains about
$83\%$ of the variation in the group-mean outcomes.

**Step 6: a check on the projection matrix.** The hat matrix is
$H=\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{A}^\top\mathbf{A})^{-1}\mathbf{A}^\top$. Its $i$-th diagonal entry, with row
$\mathbf{a}^{(i)}=(1,i)$, is
$H_{ii}=\mathbf{a}^{(i)}(\mathbf{A}^\top\mathbf{A})^{-1}\mathbf{a}^{(i)\top}=\tfrac1{20}(30-20i+4i^2)$,
giving $H_{11}=\tfrac{14}{20}=0.7$, $H_{22}=\tfrac{6}{20}=0.3$, $H_{33}=0.3$, $H_{44}=0.7$. Their sum is
$\operatorname{tr}(H)=2=p$, confirming @cor-projection-trace-rank. These diagonal entries are the
**leverages**: the end groups (covariate values $1$ and $4$) sit farther from the covariate mean and so pull
harder on the fitted line, exactly the influence diagnostic referenced for trial arms in later chapters.
One also checks $H^2=H$ and $H^\top=H$ on this $4\times4$ matrix, so $H$ is indeed the orthogonal projection
onto $\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{A})$, as @thm-projection-matrix-characterization requires.

The whole calculation can be read as a dictionary between geometry and statistics.

| Object | Symbol | Value here | What it means for the data |
|---|---|---|---|
| Design columns | $\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2$ | $(1,1,1,1),\ (1,2,3,4)$ | intercept and the covariate (dose level $1$ to $4$) |
| Column space | $\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{A})$ | all straight-line vectors | every fitted pattern a line can produce |
| Coefficients | $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ | $(\tfrac12,\,1)$ | intercept $\tfrac12$, slope $1$ |
| Fitted values | $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ | $(\tfrac32,\tfrac52,\tfrac72,\tfrac92)$ | model-predicted outcomes |
| Residual | $\mathbf{r}$ | $(-\tfrac12,\tfrac12,\tfrac12,-\tfrac12)$ | unexplained part of each outcome |
| Orthogonality | $\langle\mathbf{r},\mathbf{a}_1\rangle,\langle\mathbf{r},\mathbf{a}_2\rangle$ | $0,\ 0$ | residuals sum to zero and are uncorrelated with the covariate |
| Fit quality | $R^2$ | $\tfrac56\approx0.833$ | fraction of outcome variation the line explains |

## Notes and references {#sec-ch02-notes}

The development follows the classical treatment of orthogonality, projections, least squares, and the QR
factorization in @strang2016, recast in the theorem-proof style of this book and specialized to the needs
of indirect comparison. The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality @thm-cauchy-schwarz-ip, the Gram-Schmidt process
@thm-gram-schmidt, the orthogonal decomposition @thm-orthogonal-decomposition, and the projection theorem
@thm-projection-theorem are standard, but we have given complete elementary proofs rather than citing them,
because the entire least-squares machinery of Part I and the geometric arguments of Parts IV through VI
rest on them. The intrinsic characterization of projection matrices as the symmetric idempotents
@thm-projection-matrix-characterization, the Gram-matrix lemma @lem-gram-nullspace, and the normal
equations @thm-normal-equations-geometry are the precise results Chapter 6 reuses to construct the
ordinary-least-squares estimator (@thm-ols-normal-equations, @def-hat-matrix) and to prove it best linear
unbiased (@thm-ols-blue); we deliberately proved them with no probabilistic input so that the geometry and
the statistics stay cleanly separated.

The weighted inner product $\langle\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\rangle_A=\mathbf{x}^\top A\mathbf{y}$ for
$A\succ0$ previewed after @def-inner-product, and computed on numbers in @exm-weighted-angle, is the bridge
to the Mahalanobis geometry of matching: the balancing problem solved by MAIC in Part IV and the
distance-matching estimators of Part VI are projections and minimizations in such weighted spaces, so every
theorem here transfers to them by replacing the Euclidean inner product with $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_A$.
The positive-definiteness facts used there are proved in Chapter 3 (@thm-pd-characterization), and the
numerically preferred singular value decomposition mentioned at the end of @sec-qr is the subject of
@thm-svd. Figures are described in words throughout, and the numerical examples (@exm-two-arm-running,
@exm-weighted-angle, @exm-gs-two-vectors, @exm-complement-r3, @exm-projection-line, @exm-rank-deficient,
@exm-two-arm-fit) are chosen so the reader can draw each picture and recompute each step by hand.

No result in this chapter has a counterpart in the `ITC_Coq` Coq development, whose `theories/` formalize
the causal and population-adjustment layers rather than the underlying linear algebra; accordingly no
`[machine-checked: ...]` tag is attached here. The projection theorem and the normal equations are the
load-bearing prerequisites for the formalized results that begin in Part II.

## Exercises {#sec-ch02-exercises}

Exercises marked with a star ($\star$) have a full solution in Appendix F. The first few are short warm-ups
and interpretation prompts; the computational exercises and proofs follow.

::: {#exr-warmup-column-space}
## Warm-up: the column space in words
For the two-arm design $\mathbf{X}$ of @exm-two-arm-running, describe the column space $\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})$
in one English sentence (no formulas), and state which single vector in $\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{X})$ is closest
to the data $\mathbf{y}=(1,3,6,8)^\top$. You should not need any calculation beyond reading the example.
:::

::: {#exr-warmup-fitted-coef}
## Warm-up: fitted values versus coefficients
In @exm-rank-deficient the coefficients $(\beta_0,\beta_{\mathrm{F}},\beta_{\mathrm{M}})$ are not unique, yet
the fitted values are. In one or two sentences, explain to a colleague why dropping one of the two sex
indicators makes the remaining coefficients unique without changing any predicted outcome.
:::

::: {#exr-project-twice}
## Warm-up: why projecting twice changes nothing
Explain in words why an orthogonal projection $P$ satisfies $P^2=P$ (the idempotent property), by appealing
to the projection theorem @thm-projection-theorem rather than to matrix algebra. (Hint: where does
$P\mathbf{v}$ already live, and what is the closest point in $\mathcal{M}$ to a vector that is already in
$\mathcal{M}$?)
:::

::: {#exr-two-arm-trial}
## A two-arm trial by hand
A trial has two control patients with outcomes $1$ and $3$ and two treated patients with outcomes $5$ and
$7$. Using an intercept and a treatment indicator, write down the design matrix $\mathbf{X}$ and outcome
vector $\mathbf{y}$, solve the normal equations @eq-normal-equations for $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}=(\hat\beta_0,\hat\beta_1)^\top$,
and interpret $\hat\beta_1$ as the estimated treatment effect. Then report the fitted values and residual,
verify that the residual is orthogonal to both columns of $\mathbf{X}$, and compute $R^2$. (You should find
$\hat\beta_1$ equal to the difference of arm means and $R^2=0.8$.)
:::

::: {#exr-weighted-angle-compute}
## A weighted angle
With the weighted inner product of @exm-weighted-angle, $A=\operatorname{diag}(2,1)$, compute
$\langle\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\rangle_A$, $\|\mathbf{x}\|_A$, $\|\mathbf{y}\|_A$, and the weighted angle for
$\mathbf{x}=(1,0)^\top$ and $\mathbf{y}=(1,1)^\top$. Compare with the Euclidean angle between the same two
vectors and state in one sentence what the weighting did.
:::

::: {#exr-gram-schmidt-r3}
## Gram-Schmidt by hand
Apply the Gram-Schmidt process @thm-gram-schmidt to the vectors
$\mathbf{a}_1=(1,1,0)^\top$, $\mathbf{a}_2=(1,0,1)^\top$, $\mathbf{a}_3=(0,1,1)^\top$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$ with
the Euclidean inner product. Report the orthonormal vectors $\mathbf{q}_1,\mathbf{q}_2,\mathbf{q}_3$ and
verify that $\langle\mathbf{q}_i,\mathbf{q}_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}$.
:::

::: {#exr-projection-plane}
## A projection matrix onto a plane
Let $\mathcal{M}=\operatorname{span}\{(1,1,1)^\top,(1,0,-1)^\top\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^3$. Compute the
orthogonal projection matrix $P_{\mathcal{M}}$ using @eq-hat-matrix, verify directly that $P_{\mathcal{M}}^\top=P_{\mathcal{M}}$
and $P_{\mathcal{M}}^2=P_{\mathcal{M}}$, and confirm $\operatorname{tr}(P_{\mathcal{M}})=2$. Then find
$P_{\mathcal{M}}\mathbf{v}$ and the residual for $\mathbf{v}=(3,0,0)^\top$, and check the residual is
orthogonal to both spanning vectors.
:::

::: {#exr-line-fit}
## Least squares and $R^2$
Fit a straight line by least squares to the points $(x_i,y_i)\in\{(0,1),(1,1),(2,2),(3,2)\}$ by solving the
normal equations @eq-normal-equations. Report $\hat{\mathbf{x}}=(\hat\beta_0,\hat\beta_1)^\top$, the fitted
values, the residual vector, $\mathrm{RSS}$, $\mathrm{TSS}$, and $R^2$, and verify the residual is orthogonal
to both columns of the design matrix.
:::

::: {#exr-qr-backsub}
## Least squares by QR
For the design matrix and data of @exr-line-fit, compute the reduced QR factorization $\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{R}$
with positive diagonal, then solve $\mathbf{R}\hat{\mathbf{x}}=\mathbf{Q}^\top\mathbf{b}$ by back-substitution
and confirm you recover the same $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$.
:::

::: {#exr-double-complement}
## The double complement
Let $\mathcal{M}$ be a subspace of a finite-dimensional inner product space $V$. Prove
$(\mathcal{M}^\perp)^\perp=\mathcal{M}$ directly from @thm-orthogonal-decomposition, without invoking the
dimension count of @cor-complement-dimension. (Hint: take $\mathbf{v}\in(\mathcal{M}^\perp)^\perp$, write its
orthogonal decomposition relative to $\mathcal{M}$, and show the $\mathcal{M}^\perp$-part is $\mathbf{0}$.)
:::

::: {#exr-bessel}
## Bessel's inequality
Let $\{\mathbf{q}_1,\dots,\mathbf{q}_k\}$ be an orthonormal set (not necessarily a basis) in an inner product
space, and let $\mathbf{v}$ be any vector. Prove Bessel's inequality
$\sum_{i=1}^k\langle\mathbf{v},\mathbf{q}_i\rangle^2\le\|\mathbf{v}\|^2$, with equality if and only if
$\mathbf{v}\in\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf{q}_1,\dots,\mathbf{q}_k\}$. (Hint: project onto the span and apply
@thm-pythagoras.)
:::

::: {#exr-trace-idempotent}
## Trace of a general idempotent
Let $P\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ be idempotent, $P^2=P$, but not necessarily symmetric (an *oblique*
projection). Prove that $\operatorname{rank}(P)=\operatorname{tr}(P)$ and that the eigenvalues of $P$ lie in
$\{0,1\}$. Show by a $2\times2$ example that such a $P$ need not be an orthogonal projection, and that for it
$\|P\mathbf{v}\|>\|\mathbf{v}\|$ is possible.
:::

::: {#exr-parallelogram}
## Parallelogram law and polarization (starred)
$\star$ Let $\|\cdot\|$ be the norm induced by an inner product. Prove the **parallelogram law**
$$
\|\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}\|^2+\|\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v}\|^2=2\|\mathbf{u}\|^2+2\|\mathbf{v}\|^2,
$$
and the **polarization identity**
$\langle\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\rangle=\tfrac14\bigl(\|\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}\|^2-\|\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v}\|^2\bigr)$.
Deduce that the inner product is uniquely determined by its norm, and explain why the $\ell^1$ norm
$\|\mathbf{x}\|_1=\sum_i|x_i|$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$ cannot arise from any inner product. (Solution in Appendix F.)
:::

::: {#exr-oblique-vs-orthogonal}
## When is an idempotent an orthogonal projection? (starred)
$\star$ Let $P\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ be idempotent ($P^2=P$). Prove that the following are equivalent:
(i) $P$ is symmetric; (ii) $P$ is the orthogonal projection onto $\mathcal{C}(P)$; (iii)
$\|P\mathbf{v}\|\le\|\mathbf{v}\|$ for every $\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{R}^n$; (iv) $\mathcal{C}(P)\perp\mathcal{N}(P)$.
(Hint: for (iii) $\Rightarrow$ (i), decompose an arbitrary $\mathbf{v}$ using $\mathbb{R}^n=\mathcal{C}(P)\oplus\mathcal{N}(P)$,
which holds for any idempotent, and test the contraction inequality on $\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{m}+t\mathbf{w}$ as
$t\to\infty$.) (Solution in Appendix F.)
:::
